Ensemble weights for growing degree-day methods

Source: R/ensemble.R
gdd_ensemble_weights.Rd

Usage

gdd_ensemble_weights(
  x,
  level = "daily",
  methods = NULL,
  scheme = c("stacking", "bma", "akaike"),
  cv = TRUE,
  tol = 1e-10,
  max_iter = 10000L
)

Arguments

x

Validation results: an object from validate_station(), a list of such objects (one per station; names are used as station labels), or a data frame with columns method, estimate and observed, and optionally station, season, index and level.

level

Level of the estimates to combine: "daily", "monthly" or "gridded" (see validate_station()). Weights for daily extremes are not valid for monthly climatologies and vice versa.

methods

Member methods. NULL (default) uses every daily degree_days() method present at level; estimates from hourly reconstructions ("hourly_linvill", "hourly_sine") are not members because they cannot be computed by degree_days().

scheme

"stacking", "bma" or "akaike".

cv

Assess the ensemble by leave-one-group-out cross-validation?

tol, max_iter

Convergence tolerance and maximum number of iterations of the solvers.

Value

An object of class "gdd_ensemble_weights": a list with weights (named, non-negative, summing to one), scheme, level, base, upper and cutoff (when known), sigma (BMA error standard deviation, degrees C day), n_cases, n_groups, fit (metrics of the ensemble and of each member on the estimation cases), cv (cross-validated metrics of the ensemble, or NULL) and, for scheme = "akaike", aic (AIC, \(\Delta\) and weight per method).

Details

Estimates the weights of a growing degree-day ensemble from validation results, that is, from estimates of each method compared with values computed from observed hourly temperature (see validate_station()). The weights are then used by degree_days() with method = "ensemble", by gdd_ensemble() and by thermify() and thermify_rast() through gdd_weights.

thermify does not ship default weights: they depend on the climate, the base temperature and the data available (daily extremes or monthly climatologies), so they must be estimated from stations that represent the area of use.

The ensemble is experimental: its interface may change once it has been assessed with observed station networks.

Schemes

  • "stacking" (default) chooses non-negative weights that sum to one and minimise the squared error of the weighted estimate (Breiman 1996; Yao et al. 2018). The member methods have no fitted parameters, so their estimates are already out-of-sample predictions and can be stacked directly. Stacking is robust when no method is "true" and when members are nearly identical: their weight is shared but the prediction does not change.

  • "bma" is Bayesian model averaging with Gaussian errors and a common standard deviation, fitted by expectation-maximisation (Raftery et al. 2005). Each weight is the posterior probability that a method is the best description of the observations, so weights follow each method's likelihood. Without bias correction BMA tends to concentrate the weight on the least biased method, and nearly identical methods split it.

  • "akaike" uses Akaike weights (Burnham & Anderson 2002): \(w_k \propto \exp(-\Delta_k / 2)\), where \(\Delta_k\) is the difference between the AIC of method \(k\) and the smallest AIC. The AIC of each method uses Gaussian errors with its own maximum-likelihood variance, \(AIC_k = n \log(2\pi\hat\sigma_k^2) + n + 2p\), with \(p = 1\) (the variance): the member methods have no fitted parameters, so the penalty is the same for all and the weights reduce to relative likelihoods, \(w_k \propto \hat\sigma_k^{-n}\). With many cases they concentrate almost all the weight on the method with the smallest mean squared error, so they select rather than combine. The AIC table is returned in aic.

Assessment

When the cases come from more than one station (or, with a single station, from more than one season), the ensemble is assessed by leave-one-group-out cross-validation: the weights are re-estimated without each group and used to predict it. Compare cv with the metrics of the best single method before using the ensemble: when the members share the same systematic error, weighting cannot remove it.

References

Burnham, K. P., & Anderson, D. R. (2002). Model Selection and Multimodel Inference: A Practical Information-Theoretic Approach (2nd ed.). Springer. doi:10.1007/b97636

Breiman, L. (1996). Stacked regressions. Machine Learning, 24, 49-64. doi:10.1007/BF00117832

Raftery, A. E., Gneiting, T., Balabdaoui, F., & Polakowski, M. (2005). Using Bayesian model averaging to calibrate forecast ensembles. Monthly Weather Review, 133(5), 1155-1174. doi:10.1175/MWR2906.1

Yao, Y., Vehtari, A., Simpson, D., & Gelman, A. (2018). Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions. Bayesian Analysis, 13(3), 917-1007. doi:10.1214/17-BA1091

See also

gdd_ensemble(), validate_station()

Examples

# Illustration with made-up validation results (not real data): the
# observed totals lie between the averaging and the sine estimates.
val <- data.frame(
  station = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 6),
  season = rep(rep(c(2020, 2021), each = 3), 3),
  method = rep(c("average", "single_sine", "single_triangle"), 6),
  estimate = c(950, 1010, 990, 1200, 1270, 1240, 870, 935, 910,
               1020, 1080, 1060, 1110, 1180, 1150, 990, 1050, 1030),
  observed = rep(c(985, 1245, 905, 1055, 1150, 1025), each = 3))
w <- gdd_ensemble_weights(val)
w
#> GDD ensemble weights (stacking, level "daily")
#> 6 cases in 3 station group(s)
#> 
#>     single_sine         average single_triangle 
#>           0.585           0.415           0.000 
#> 
#> Fit on the estimation cases:
#>           method n      bias    mae   rmse
#>         ensemble 6   0.04364  1.391  2.101
#>          average 6 -37.50000 37.500 37.694
#>      single_sine 6  26.66667 26.667 26.771
#>  single_triangle 6   2.50000  4.167  4.564
#> 
#> Cross-validated ensemble (leave one station out):
#>    method n     bias   mae  rmse
#>  ensemble 6 -0.01417 2.107 2.946
degree_days(c(5, 8), c(22, 25), method = "ensemble", weights = w,
            base = 10)
#> [1] 4.195342 6.672432
